posts.text: NEW BIS RULE – The BIS rule tightens US AI-chip export controls to stop Chinese companies bypassing restrictions by renting computing power from overseas data centres rather than buying chips directly. Released yesterday by the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, it was written by and at the direction of Treasury and the National Security Council. It formally rescinds the earlier, unenforced AI Diffusion Rule.It introduces licensing requirements for advanced chips and servers used by data centres worldwide to provide substantial computing capacity to Chinese and other restricted companies. It also adds chip-export licensing requirements for Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil, and tightens customer checks and foundry controls, with certain exemptions for US-headquartered recipients and commercial recommendation systems. The aim is to close the offshore-compute loophole and protect US national security. The likely impact is higher compliance costs and greater uncertainty for chip suppliers and cloud operators, potentially more expensive or restricted access to advanced compute for Chinese AI developers, and delays to affected chip shipments and data-centre projects—not a blanket ban on overseas AI investment. Tighter compute access is also seen as a risk to AI model training and Chinese cloud revenue growth. Licence approvals will be considered case by case.

I'm excited to share; I'm looking for two people to join me at Nafas Foundation! Indonesia's air quality science and technology non-profit organisation.

Over the past few years, air quality in Indonesia increasingly become national conversation. Unfortunately, it has once again become Southeast Asia's primary concerns this year.

When I first started air quality, I was fascinated by the science itself (as an atmospheric science nerd). Over time, curiosity evolved into something crucial: understanding how science and technology interact with society. 

📖  The very reason, I chose to study Science in Society. What began as an enthusiasm for generating new form of knowledge, was evolved into a different set of social-discipline questions:

What happens after the evidence exists? 
What happens after the data is produced? 
How do people make sense of it? 
How do institutions respond to it? 
And what helps turn knowledge into action?

These questions led me to moments of reflection on what works best in Indonesia.

While air pollution may be a shared challenge, the air we experience is deeply local, especially in Indonesia, where evidence is effective when it is grounded in local realities and connected to local needs, capacities, and priorities.

In a country as diverse as Indonesia, with its rich cultures, histories, languages, and lived realities, every place has its own context, ecosystem, priorities, capacities, and challenges. Solutions work in one place less likely 'simply' be transplanted to another. The understanding of local realities with the people who know the realities, works best for a lasting progress.

At Nafas Foundation, we're investing in a locally led approach to air quality, strengthening community-based outdoor monitoring networks (continuing five years of local volunteers) and working alongside communities, researchers, governments, and partners to build a better understanding of local air quality from the ground up. Increasingly, we're seeing local knowledge serve as a compass for a collaborative decision-making at local government level!

Two new data centres opened in Jakarta this month. Each one needs a team that can run it every hour of the year.

On 1 November, LG CNS completed a 30 MW AI data centre in Jakarta for KMG, a joint venture of Sinar Mas Group and Korea Investment Real Asset Management. LG CNS says customers took the full capacity before construction finished. Later phases could take incoming power to 400 MW.

On 3 November, NTT DATA opened its Jakarta 2 Annex, with 12 MW of IT capacity.

The buildings get the headlines. The people who keep them running get less attention. A site that promises uptime all year needs a site head, engineers who know power and cooling, and someone who can manage clients on strict contracts.

Every new operator will look first at the people who have already run a facility like this. That group is small, so it helps to look further.

Two suggestions for companies building or expanding in this sector.

Look at adjacent industries. Power plants, large manufacturing sites and telecom networks also run critical equipment around the clock, and their leaders know what an outage costs.

Hire the site leader before commissioning. That person should help choose the team that will run the site, not inherit one.

We are pleased to announce Dewi Muliana, Head of the Center for Green Industry, Ministry of Industry of the Republic of Indonesia, as a distinguished speaker at the 4th Carbon Digital Conference 2026 (CDC 2026). As global markets increasingly demand lower-carbon products and more transparent supply chains, Indonesia's industrial sector faces a critical challenge: How can manufacturers reduce emissions while maintaining competitiveness, attracting investment, and supporting economic growth?

From steel, cement, and chemicals to nickel processing, pulp and paper, and other energy-intensive industries, the transition toward greener manufacturing is becoming an increasingly important business and policy priority. At CDC 2026, Dewi will bring an important government perspective to the broader conversation on industrial decarbonization and the development of Indonesia's carbon economy.

Key issues include:
- Green Industry Transformation: Accelerating the adoption of sustainable manufacturing practices and green industry standards.
- Industrial Decarbonization: Reducing emissions through energy efficiency, cleaner technologies, and low-carbon production.
- Carbon Accounting & Transparency: Strengthening emissions measurement, reporting, and verification across industrial operations.
- Green Investment & Carbon Finance: Exploring financing mechanisms to support industrial transformation and emerging low-carbon technologies.
- Global Competitiveness: Preparing Indonesian industries for evolving international climate requirements and demand for lower-carbon products.

As carbon-related requirements increasingly influence international trade, investment decisions, and supply-chain relationships, Indonesian manufacturers must navigate the transition toward cleaner production while managing costs and protecting their market positions. Can carbon markets, climate finance, and industrial policy work together to accelerate this transformation? That is among the important questions to be explored at CDC 2026, the largest carbon project developers convention in the region.
